articles.title: Department of War Publishes Second Release of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Files on WAR.GOV/UFO
articles.summary: Prediction markets on Kalshi and Polymarket show a 4.1% aggregate probability that the U.S. will definitively confirm extraterrestrial life or technology before 2027, with a 95.9% probability that it will not. The Pentagon has released five batches of UAP records through August 7 2026 via the PURSUE system, adding 162 files and videos, but none of the releases contains an official statement that extraterrestrial life exists. Senior officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and independent researchers have provided context and analysis of the records, but their statements and the missing technical data in sensor videos do not meet the market’s settlement criteria for a “Yes” outcome. The market’s “Yes” trigger requires a definitive declaration by a qualifying U.S. official or agency by December 31 2026; no such declaration has occurred, and the White House’s domain registrations and public releases are not evidence of imminent confirmation. After the fifth release, the aggregate “Yes” probability fell from 6.2% to 3.9% by August 27, indicating that the market remains skeptical of an official alien confirmation before 2027.

articles.summary: The Pentagon’s new waiver allows current and former service members, personnel and contractors with access to UAP‑related National Defense Information to speak openly about what they know, superseding nondisclosure and Special Access Program agreements. Avi Loeb, head of the UAP Science Advisory Council, said the information would still need to be disclosed behind closed doors, so some details could remain off‑limits. He noted the waiver could enable disclosures on recovered non‑human craft, but that depends on the nature of the information and that the government may still hold undisclosed evidence. The waiver is seen as a potential key step toward full UAP disclosure, though it is unclear what evidence the government actually possesses and what will remain classified.

Avi Loeb, head of the UAP Science Advisory Council, said that while the waiver permits disclosure, the information would still need to be presented behind closed doors, meaning some details could remain off‑limits. Loeb added that the waiver could enable disclosure of recovered non‑human craft depending on the nature of the information and that he hopes President Trump’s declassification directive will apply to non‑human‑made technologies. He emphasized that new firsthand accounts and scientific evidence could help determine whether the government possesses non‑human‑made technologies, and that if the government holds undisclosed tangible evidence, the waivers could be extremely important. The article notes that the waiver is seen as a major step toward full UAP disclosure, but it is unclear exactly what information will ultimately be released.
